title: Australia’s $150 million embarrassment at climate talks
transcript:
Speaker 1: Today's biggest news from The Australian. I'm Claire Harvey with the front's afternoon headlines. A global climate summit that's cost billions of dollars has collapsed in embarrassing failure and Australia is getting the blame and a $ 150 million bill for taxpayers. Council of the Parties, or COP, is an annual United Nations conference which is supposed to guide progress towards achieving the Paris Agreement. In Paris, countries agreed in 2015 to attempt to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees above pre-industrial levels. That was what this year's COP31 was supposed to do. Australia tried to get the rights to host the event in Adelaide, but got outbid by Turkey. And as a consolation, our Energy Minister Chris Bowen was appointed to lead negotiations. Here's what happened. A number of countries, including Australia, wanted the COP31 countries to agree to a document that explicitly said they were agreeing to transition away from fossil fuels and commit to ensuring that by 2035, 35% of energy use comes from electricity, not fossil fuels. But oil-producing countries, including from the Middle East, didn't want any mention of fossil fuels. Russia said it would be a meaningless slogan and could risk creating so-called fuel poverty if the transition wasn't managed properly. Multiple drafts of the text included mention of fossil fuels, but on Sunday the final draft didn't contain any mention, and so there was no agreement and no document was signed. The countries also failed to come to an agreement on other issues they'd been working on, like financial assistance to help poor countries adapt to climate change. Something else they couldn't agree on? a form of words about that 1.5 degree temperature rise from the Paris Agreement way back in 2015. The UN now says it's going to be more like 2.8 degrees by 2100 on the current trajectory. But countries at COP31 couldn't agree on recommitting to the 1.5 degree figure or even acknowledging that the world is not going to meet that target. Here's Chris Bowen.
Speaker 2: I haven't slept for the last three nights, been negotiating all the way through, but more importantly, people... on delegations, came at it and gave it everything they had, but it didn't work.
Speaker 1: He was the most influential and the most entertaining figure in Australian music for decades, and Ian Molly Meldrum is being remembered today after his death at 83 as a true champion of creativity. Meldrum started out as a music journalist, hosting the ABC music show Countdown for more than a decade. and then working as a producer and impresario, including regular TV and radio appearances. In 1977, the normally relaxed and self-assured Meldrum acted all nervous in an interview with the then Prince Charles. And now we come to the most important part of tonight's program. I'm sweating like a pig. Oh, f * * *. And 40 years later, the now king roasted Meldrum right back. I suddenly learned some interesting new Australian words from Mr Meldrum, and... If he could have read my mind, he would have learned some interesting new English words from me. It only seems like yesterday. I wish it were tomorrow. I'd cancel it. Check out those stories live right now at theaustralian.com.au. And come back to the front first thing in the morning for our look at a bitter civil war ripping apart the Greens with broader implications for the whole of Australia. Who gets to call themselves Indigenous? That's right here Tuesday morning.
